images.caption: Royal Air Force (RAF) BAC Jet Provost T5A registration XW323, c/n EEP/JP/987.  Built 1970 and delivered in December to RAF Cranwell.  During 1971 it was one of two Jet Provosts allocated for pilot training of Prince Charles (Flt Lt The Prince of Wales) and was known as 'Golden Eagle Two'.  It remained in use at Cranwell until 1991, when it moved to No. 1 Flying Training School RAF (1FTS) at RAF Linton-on-Ouse, from where it retired in October 1992.  In December of that year it was transported to Hendon where it remains on display in the Historic Main Hangars, RAF Museum, Hendon, London, UK.  22-3-2015.

Retired in 1989 and with the fire section at RAF Church Fenton by May 1990 with the maintenance serial 9036M.  Joined the museum in 1995. images.caption: Royal Air Force (RAF) Percival Provost T1 registration WV562, c/n PAC/56/F/108.  Built 1954.  Flew with 22 Flying Training School (22FTS) at RAF Syerston, which was later renumbered as No. 1 Flying Training School RAF (1FTS) and moved to RAF Linton-on-Ouse.  Retired in 1959 as replaced by Jet Provosts.  Used for ground instruction at RAF Henlow and RAF Cranwell until moved to Cosford museum in 1979.  During 2014 she was temporarily painted in Sultan of Oman Air Force colours for an exhibition at Hendon.  She has now returned to Cosford and her RAF colours.  Currently on display in Hangar 1 at the RAF Museum Cosford, Shropshire, UK.  14th August 2016.

images.caption:
Grimsby Dock Tower
Pevsner says "THE DOCK TOWER, 1851-2 by J.W.Wild, is the most memorable building in Grimsby, a beacon for many miles...inspired by Siena Town Hall, but the crowning minaret is oriental. It was built as part of the hydraulic system to open the lock gates and operate cranes, the first major dock to use hydraulic power for this purpose. Of red brick, 309ft tall, taller than Lincoln Cathedral, it rises in an unbroken line to the corbelled-out top, surmounted by a further section again with a corbelled-out top...".
Note that the Grimsby tower isn't a hydraulic accumulator (it's in the category because it's an important part of their history). Towers such as Grimsby achieved high pressures simply by their height, expensive though these were to construct. It was soon realised that a pressurised cistern with a heavy iron or concrete weight on it gave the same results, at much less cost.
Photo taken from the footbridge on the A180 flyover.
